vignette:
Mere Tuilagi is a 63-year-old Fijian-American woman who works as a project manager for a regional construction firm in Phoenix, Arizona. She has been married for thirty-four years and describes her husband as her closest confidant, though she acknowledges that even he cannot fully reach her now. She was referred for psychological assessment following a conversation with her primary care physician, who noted her persistent reluctance to attend follow-up appointments and her visible distress during routine examinations.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Mere was admitted to hospital in acute respiratory failure secondary to a rapidly progressing bacterial pneumonia that had been initially misdiagnosed as a seasonal chest infection. What began as a week of fatigue and shortness of breath ended with Mere losing consciousness at home and waking in an intensive care unit with a central line running into her neck, an oxygen mask pressing against her face, and her wrists loosely restrained to prevent her from pulling at the drip lines she could feel but not see. She later learned she had been unconscious for four days. What she remembered was more fragmented: the cold pressure of the cannula entering the back of her hand, the particular angle at which her neck was turned against a pillow she could not adjust, the sound of an alarm she could not interpret, and a sustained sensation of drowning from the inside.

In the weeks after her discharge, Mere returned to work earlier than her doctors recommended, telling herself that structure would help. For a time, it did. But her office environment, where project timelines are reviewed in long team meetings, became unexpectedly difficult to navigate. When colleagues raised topics about hospital delays in construction supply chains - a recurring industry problem - or when conversations drifted toward illness, injury, or medical costs, Mere found herself abruptly unable to follow the thread of the discussion. She described it not as distraction but as a sudden and total absence, as though the room continued without her. What frightened her most in those moments was that she could not find words for what was happening to her. The experience of the ICU had not organized itself into a story she could tell; it existed instead as sensation and position, as the specific weight of her body immobilized and the cold tracking of fluid into her vein. When the memory returned, it did not arrive as a recollection. It arrived as the thing itself - the smell of antiseptic, the restraint at her wrists, the drowning - and her body assumed the posture of those four days without her choosing it.

She had come to believe that her body had fundamentally failed her, and that it might do so again without warning. She no longer trusted the signals it sent. A tight chest after climbing stairs was not fatigue; it was the beginning of something catastrophic. She had quietly stopped attending her scheduled follow-up appointments, finding reasons to reschedule, and when her husband accompanied her to a routine blood draw, she became rigid the moment the phlebotomist uncapped the needle. She asked to leave before the draw was completed. She did not explain to her husband why, because she could not explain it to herself in language.

At work, she had grown short-tempered in ways that surprised people who had known her for years. An unexpected hand on her shoulder from a colleague had once prompted a sharp, audible gasp and a response that she later described as mortifying. She had difficulty sustaining concentration across the long planning documents that were central to her role, and a project she had been managing for two years had slipped in ways her supervisor had begun to notice.

Mere had come to feel that the woman who had managed complex builds and raised two children and cooked elaborate Sunday meals had been replaced by someone she did not recognize and could not trust. She had told her husband, in a rare moment of disclosure, that she felt her life as she had known it was simply gone. What finally brought her to seek help was not any single incident but the accumulation of distance - from her work, from her husband, from the body she lived in. She arrived at the intake appointment hoping, above all, to be believed.
